summary:
We built a web dashboard over NASA’s Physical Science Informatics repository. From two raw ACME records, PSI-10 and PSI-159, we assembled a single clean dataset of 697 ignition tests flown aboard the International Space Station between 2019 and 2022, covering four gaseous fuels and two burner configurations. Every flow reading was corrected with its gas-specific calibration factor, and every change documented so the cleaning is reproducible.

On that dataset we trained a predictive flammability model that estimates ignition probability from the chamber atmosphere and the burner flows, using physically grounded variables such as the jet expressed in oxygen-equivalent liters.

The dashboard has three parts: a preventive risk monitor with presets for ISS and exploration atmospheres, a searchable explorer that compares investigations and lets every prediction be audited against the recorded outcome, and an assistant that answers questions in plain language.
details:
What it does and how it works. The project is a web dashboard that turns raw NASA combustion records into a usable fire-safety tool. The pipeline has three stages. First, a Python script reads two ACME workbooks from NASA’s Physical Science Informatics repository, PSI-10 and PSI-159, and merges them into one clean dataset of 697 ignition tests between 2019 and 2022, across 46 test days, four gaseous fuels and two burner configurations. Each flow reading is converted to real delivered volume using the gas-specific correction factor of the mass-flow controller, invalid rows are removed, and every change is written to a log so the cleaning is reproducible. Second, a logistic model is trained on that dataset and exported to JSON. Third, a React application loads that JSON and evaluates the model directly in the browser, so the dashboard runs with no server and no network connection.

The dashboard has three sections. A preventive risk monitor estimates the ignition probability of any scenario the user sets, with presets for ISS conditions and for the reduced-pressure, oxygen-enriched atmospheres proposed for exploration vehicles, plus a heat map showing how risk moves when two parameters change at once. A searchable explorer lists every test with its conditions, its real outcome, and the model’s blind prediction side by side, so any claim can be audited. An assistant answers questions about the data in plain language.

Benefits and impact. Researchers, engineers and students can move from a spreadsheet of raw voltages to an interpretable risk estimate in seconds, and can ask what would happen in atmospheres that have never been tested in orbit. Because every prediction sits next to the recorded outcome, the tool invites scrutiny rather than blind trust, which matters for a safety application.

Tools. Python with pandas, NumPy, scikit-learn and SciPy for cleaning, training and validation. React 18 with Vite 5 for the interface, with react and react-dom as the only runtime dependencies; every chart is hand-written SVG, with no charting library. A single-file build produces one self-contained HTML page that opens offline with a double click.

What makes it creative. The model is not a black box fitted blindly. Its coefficients are constrained by physics: more reactant and more oxidizer-equivalent jet must raise the probability, while inert nitrogen and carbon dioxide must lower it. Those bounds are enforced during optimization. Oxygen and fuel are unified into a single “chamber reactant” variable so both flame configurations share one model, and the burner jet is expressed in oxygen-equivalent liters using each fuel’s stoichiometry, which lets ethane and butane be compared fairly despite needing 3.5 and 6.5 oxygen molecules respectively.

Factors considered. Validation holds out each test day in full, so the model is never scored on a session it has seen. The dashboard refuses to extrapolate beyond the tested range, and a physical rule returns zero when fuel or oxidizer is absent.
